sources.title: C. Krattenthaler, "Lattice Path Enumeration", ch. 10 of the Handbook of Enumerative Combinatorics

contents.name: 10.1. Introduction (step sets, paths, the methods surveyed)
10.2. Lattice paths without restrictions
10.3. Linear boundaries of slope 1
Theorem 10.3.1 (paths from (a,b) to (c,d) staying strictly above a line of slope 1, by reflection)
Corollary 10.3.2 (the Catalan numbers count such paths, and their generating function)
Theorem 10.3.3 (paths confined between two parallel lines of slope 1)
contents.reason: A two-sided boundary needs iterated reflection in two lines, producing an alternating sum over the infinite dihedral group generated by them; each summand vanishes for large index but the vanishing has to be proved, and this page fixes only one boundary. The one-sided reflection lemma it builds is the ingredient, not the result.

contents.name: Theorem 10.3.4 (the same two-boundary count in its second, generating-function form)
contents.reason: The generating-function form of the two-boundary count needs the transfer-matrix presentation of paths in a strip, which is machinery for a page about paths in a strip and is not developed here; the Catalan development needs only the single boundary at level -1.

contents.name: 10.4. Simple paths with linear boundaries of rational slope, I
Theorem 10.4.1 (paths from (0,0) to (r,s) with r, s coprime staying strictly below the line sx = ry)
contents.reason: The coprime rational-slope count is the cycle lemma applied to a word whose letters take the two values 1 and -r/s scaled to integers; carrying the coprimality bookkeeping needs the general mu-step version of every path definition on this page, which would double the definitional weight for one count the Catalan development never uses.

contents.name: Lemma 10.4.3 (Spitzer's lemma)
contents.reason: Spitzer states the cyclic-shift count for sequences of REAL numbers, where "exactly k good shifts" is replaced by a statement about ties among partial sums. This page proves the integer form, which is what every application here needs, and the real form would require an argument about ties that has no consumer.

contents.name: Theorem 10.4.5 (paths from (0,0) to (c,d) staying weakly below x = mu y)
contents.reason: This is the mu-generalisation of the ballot count. It needs the step set {(1,0),(0,1)} replaced by one whose down-steps drop mu units, which changes the discrete change-of-side lemma this page proves for unit steps; the change is real mathematics, not notation, and it belongs with the rational-slope development rather than beside the Catalan numbers.

contents.name: Lemma 10.4.6 (the cycle lemma)
Theorem 10.4.7 (paths between two points with a boundary of rational slope)
contents.reason: The two-endpoint rational-slope count composes Theorem 10.4.5 with a translation argument, so it inherits exactly the mu-step machinery declined above and adds a second endpoint to track.

contents.name: 10.13. Non-intersecting lattice paths
Theorem 10.13.1 (Lindström–Gessel–Viennot, for a directed acyclic graph with weights)
Corollary 10.13.2 (the determinant form for a compatible configuration of starts and ends)
Theorem 10.13.3 (non-intersecting paths and the Jacobi–Trudi determinant for semistandard tableaux)
contents.reason: The tableau reading of the determinant needs semistandard Young tableaux and Schur functions, and symmetric functions are not among this page’s declared prerequisites; the lattice-path half of the statement is exactly Theorem 10.13.1, which is built.

contents.name: Theorem 10.13.4 (the determinant for paths with one free family of endpoints)
contents.reason: Free endpoints turn the determinant into a sum over end-point choices, which needs the Lindström framework stated for a family of end SETS rather than points; the page states the fixed-endpoint case because that is what the two-path corollary and every consumer here use.

contents.name: Theorem 10.13.5 (the Pfaffian formula for non-intersecting paths with free ends, after Stembridge)
contents.reason: A Pfaffian is a square root of a skew determinant and the library has no Pfaffian: it would have to be constructed with its sign conventions and its relation to the determinant proved before the statement could even be written.

contents.name: Corollary 10.13.6 (the Pfaffian formula for an even number of paths)
contents.reason: A specialisation of the Pfaffian theorem and therefore blocked by the same missing object; nothing else in its statement is unavailable.

contents.name: Corollary 10.13.7 (the Pfaffian formula when the starting points are also free)
contents.reason: Same Pfaffian obstruction, and it additionally needs the free-start variant of the Lindström framework declined at Theorem 10.13.4.

contents.name: Theorem 10.13.8 (the number of non-intersecting path families with prescribed turn data)
contents.reason: This counts families by their turn statistics, which needs the turn-enumeration apparatus of §10.14; that apparatus is a development of its own and no result on this page consumes it.

contents.name: Theorem 10.13.9 (a determinant evaluation for paths with a shifted boundary)
contents.reason: The evaluation is an explicit product formula obtained by row reduction inside a determinant of binomial coefficients; the determinant identity itself is the content, and it belongs with determinant evaluations rather than with the path bijection this page proves.

contents.name: Theorem 10.13.10 (the weighted Lindström–Gessel–Viennot theorem with a general weight function)
contents.reason: The weighted form needs paths carrying weights in a commutative ring and the weight of a family defined as a product over steps; this page counts paths and never weights them, so the weighted statement would introduce an object with no consumer here.

contents.name: 10.8. Elementary results on Motzkin and Schröder paths (the step sets M = {(1,1),(1,-1),(1,0)} and S = {(1,1),(1,-1),(2,0)}; Motzkin, Schröder, Catalan and Dyck paths defined)
10.8, the reflect-rotate translation of Schröder paths into paths with steps (1,0), (0,1), (1,1) staying weakly below y = x, and the Delannoy numbers (10.6) for the unrestricted count
contents.reason: The translation is a change of model, not a result: it reflects, rotates by 45 degrees and rescales by 1/sqrt(2), which needs a plane geometry this order does not have, and the page reaches the same paths directly through its own step sets. The Delannoy numbers it points at count paths with the three steps and NO boundary, a different family from the Schröder paths built here.

contents.name: Theorem 10.8.1 (the number of Motzkin paths, and of Schröder paths, from (a,b) to (c,d) that do not pass below the x-axis, as a binomial double sum)
contents.reason: The count between two ARBITRARY endpoints is obtained in the source from the rotated model plus Theorem 10.3.1, so it inherits the change of model declined above; and the source itself says the sums do not simplify. The page needs only the endpoints on the axis, which Corollary 10.8.2 states and which the first-return decomposition reaches without any rotation.

contents.name: Corollary 10.8.2 (the number of Motzkin paths from (0,0) to (n,0) and of Schröder paths from (0,0) to (2n,0); the Motzkin numbers M_n and the large Schröder numbers S_n, with M_0 = S_0 = 1)
Equation (10.45), the closed sum for the Motzkin numbers as a binomial-weighted sum of Catalan numbers
Equation (10.46), the closed sum for the large Schröder numbers as a binomial-weighted sum of Catalan numbers
10.8, the little Schröder numbers (the large Schröder numbers halved for n >= 1, by switching the first level-step with an up-down pair)
contents.reason: Halving needs the switching map to be proved a two-to-one surjection, in particular that every Schröder path of positive half-length has a first level-step OR a first up-down pair and never both readings; the source states it as easily seen and gives no argument. The page builds the large numbers, which is what its two generating functions are about, and states neither the little numbers nor the halving.

contents.name: 10.8, decorated Motzkin paths ('histoires') and the bijections with permutations and set partitions (Biane; Foata-Zeilberger; Françon-Viennot; de Médicis-Viennot; Simion-Stanton)
contents.reason: A decorated Motzkin path carries a label on every step, so the objects are weighted paths and the results are refined enumerations of PERMUTATIONS and SET PARTITIONS, neither of which this page defines. The source gives pointers to the literature rather than statements, so there is nothing here to transcribe even if the objects were available.

contents.name: 10.9. A continued fraction for the weighted counting of Motzkin paths (the weight w: an up-step weighs 1, a level-step at height h weighs b_h, a down-step from h to h-1 weighs lambda_h)
contents.reason: The weighted counting assigns a weight per step depending on the HEIGHT at which it is taken, so the generating function lives in a polynomial ring in infinitely many indeterminates b_h and lambda_h. This page counts paths without weights, and nothing it builds needs the height-graded refinement.

contents.name: Theorem 10.9.1 (Flajolet's continued fraction for the weighted generating function of Motzkin paths in a strip 0 <= y <= k, and the infinite continued fraction obtained as k tends to infinity)
contents.reason: The finite form is an induction on the strip height over the weighted ring declined above; the infinite form is then obtained by letting k tend to infinity, which is a limit of formal continued fractions and needs the x-adic topology on the series ring, a notion the library does not develop at this order.

contents.name: Theorem 10.9.2, equation (10.49): sum_{n>=0} M_n z^n = (1 - z - sqrt(1 - 2z - 3z^2)) / (2 z^2), with M(z) = 1/(1 - z - z^2 M(z)) as the displayed intermediate
Theorem 10.9.2, equation (10.50): sum_{n>=0} S_n z^n = (1 - z - sqrt(1 - 6z + z^2)) / (2 z), the large Schröder generating function, indexed by half-length
Theorem 10.9.3 (Roblet-Viennot: the continued fraction for Dyck paths under a weight that separates a down-step following a peak from a down-step following a down-step)
contents.reason: The refined weight distinguishes a down-step by whether an up-step or a down-step precedes it, so it is a statistic on adjacent step pairs, and the result is again a continued fraction in infinitely many indeterminates. The page tracks no statistic on Dyck paths at all.

sources.title: A. Postnikov (notes by A. Lin), MIT 18.212 Algebraic Combinatorics, Spring 2019

contents.name: Example 4 (the drunk man problem, Dyck paths as +-1 sequences with nonnegative partial sums)
Proposition 5 (recurrence relation for the Catalan numbers)
Proposition 6 (generating function for the Catalan numbers)
Proposition 7 (solving the quadratic equation for the generating function)
Proposition 8 (the binomial theorem, in the generalised-exponent form used to expand the square root)
Theorem 9 (closed form for the Catalan numbers)
Claim 10 (all cyclic shifts of the relevant word are different)
Claim 11 (each necklace has a unique cut giving a good sequence)
the reflection method for the Catalan numbers (lecture of 8 February)

sources.title: D. Guichard, An Introduction to Combinatorics and Graph Theory

contents.name: 3.1 Newton's Binomial Theorem
3.2 Exponential Generating Functions
contents.reason: Exponential generating functions are the tool of the set-partition and Stirling-number development, not of the lattice-path one; every count on this page is a plain coefficient count and no labelled-structure product rule is needed.

contents.name: 3.3 Partitions of Integers
contents.reason: Integer partitions and their infinite product generating functions are a separate topic whose legitimacy rests on summability of infinite products, which this page never needs; the planned integer-partition page is where the products and Ferrers diagrams belong.

contents.name: 3.4 Recurrence Relations
3.5 Catalan Numbers: rooted binary trees and the definition of $C_n$ with $C_0=1$
3.5: the recurrence $C_n=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}C_iC_{n-i-1}$
3.5: the generating-function equation $xf^2-f+1=0$ and its solution
3.5: the closed form $C_n=\frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}$ by Newton's binomial theorem
3.5: properly matched parenthesis sequences and $\binom{2n}{n}-\binom{2n}{n+1}$
Exercise 3.5.3: a properly matched sequence factors uniquely as $(s_1)s_2$
Exercise 3.5.4: paths in an $n\times n$ staircase
Exercise 3.5.5: dividing a convex polygon into triangles by non-intersecting diagonals
Exercise 3.5.6: partitions of a set and the Bell numbers
contents.reason: Set partitions and the Bell numbers are the subject of the planned page immediately above this one in the reading order, which is where the block structure and the exponential generating function belong; nothing on this page counts a partition.

sources.title: N. Dershowitz and S. Zaks, "The Cycle Lemma and Some Applications", Europ. J. Combinatorics 11 (1990) 35–40

contents.name: 1. The Cycle Lemma (the k-dominating form for m boxes and n circles with m >= kn)
1.1 First proof (removing k boxes and a circle from the cycle)
1.2 Second proof (choosing a valid origin on the mountain range)
1.3 Other proofs (the bibliographic survey of rediscoveries and of the Lagrange-inversion analogy)
contents.reason: A bibliographic section: it states no result of its own, and the attributions it collects belong in the page’s source list rather than in an item.

contents.name: 2.1 Forests (the number of ordered forests of s t-ary trees with n internal nodes)
contents.reason: The forest count needs t-ary trees and ordered forests defined with their postorder traversal, and this page defines only binary trees; building the t-ary and forest versions would add a second tree formalism whose only consumer here is one count already obtained from the cycle lemma directly.

contents.name: 2.2 Trees (the expected height of an ordered tree is asymptotically the square root of pi n)
contents.reason: The height estimate is an asymptotic statement about a ratio of counts as n grows, so it needs limits of sequences of real numbers and Stirling-type estimates; nothing on this page is asymptotic and the bounds would rest on analysis this development deliberately does not use.

sources.title: A. Huq, Generalized Chung-Feller Theorems for Lattice Paths (PhD thesis, Brandeis University, 2009)

contents.name: Definition 1.1.1 (a lattice path with steps in a fixed finite set V of vectors in Z x Z, and its geometric realisation)
Definition 1.1.2, the Dyck paths P(n,1,0,+): paths with steps (1,1) and (1,-1) in the quarter plane, of semi-length n
Definition 1.1.2, the general families P(n,r,h) with step set {(1,1),(1,-r)} ending at ((r+1)n+h, h), and the negative paths P(n,1,0,-)
contents.reason: The down-step (1,-r) drops r units, so a path can pass from above a level to below it without meeting the level and the discrete change-of-side lemma this page proves for unit steps fails; the companion page carries exactly that failure as a counterexample. Every result of the pair is about the unit step set.

contents.name: Theorem 1.1.3 (Chung-Feller: among the binom(2n,n) paths from (0,0) to (2n,0), the number with 2k steps lying above the x-axis is independent of k and equals C_n)
2.1, the cycle lemma of Dvoretzky and Motzkin as restated there (for an n-tuple of integers from {1,0,-1,-2,...} with sum k > 0, exactly k cyclic permutations have every partial sum positive)
Theorem 2.1.1 (if a_1 + ... + a_n = 1 with every a_i an integer, then for each k with 1 <= k <= n exactly one conjugate of a has exactly k nonpositive partial sums)
Theorem 2.1.2 (the geometric reading of Theorem 2.1.1: for a path ending at height 1 there is exactly one conjugate with exactly k vertices on or below the x-axis)

Section 2.2, special vertices, and Theorem 2.2.1 (if the special vertices are preserved by cyclic shift and there are k of them, the k conjugates beginning at a special vertex realise each of 1, ..., k exactly once as the number of special vertices on or below the x-axis)
Theorem 2.3.1(1) (paths in P(n,1,1) that start with an up step, counted by the number of up steps starting on or below the x-axis: binom(2n,n)/(n+1) for each k = 1, ..., n+1)
Theorem 2.3.1(2) (paths in P(n,1,1) that start with a down step, counted by the number of down steps starting on or below the x-axis: binom(2n,n-1)/n for each k = 1, ..., n)
contents.reason: This is the interpretation of the THIRD form of the Catalan number, binom(2n,n-1)/n, which this page never states: its two proved forms are (n+1)C_n = binom(2n,n) and (2n+1)C_n = binom(2n+1,n). Building it would mean stating and proving that third form first, and the down-step reading adds no statement about the paths from (0,0) to (2n,0) that Chung-Feller is about.

contents.name: Theorem 2.3.1(3) (paths in P(n,1,1) counted by the number of vertices on or below the x-axis: binom(2n+1,n)/(2n+1) for each k = 1, ..., 2n+1)
contents.reason: A Chung-Feller statement for the (2n+1)-form of the Catalan number, over paths that end at height 1 rather than returning to the axis. The page proves the (2n+1)-form as a count of orbits and does not introduce the family of paths ending at height 1 as an object with a statistic; adding this means adding that family and its vertex statistic for one further theorem.

sources.title: L. Babai and P. Frankl, Linear Algebra Methods in Combinatorics, version 2.2.1 (November 2024)

contents.name: 1.1 Counting clubs in Oddtown
1.2 Point sets in R^n with only two distances
contents.reason: The two-distance bound is a statement about points of Euclidean space and its proof attaches a polynomial in the squared distance to each point, so it needs the Euclidean metric on R^n together with the polynomial-space argument applied to real distances rather than to set sizes; the page keeps to set systems and graphs.

contents.name: 1.3 Two solutions to a jigsaw puzzle? (the Graham–Pollak style rank argument for tilings)
contents.reason: The puzzle statement is about decompositions of a geometric board and needs the board and its pieces as objects; the linear-algebra content it exercises is already carried on this page by the Graham–Pollak theorem, so building the geometry would add an object for a repeated argument.

contents.name: 1.4 Addressing into the squashed cube (the Graham–Pollak theorem)
1.5 Beauty is rare (a counting argument bounding the number of "beautiful" objects)
contents.reason: This section is a probabilistic counting warm-up rather than a linear-algebra bound: its argument is a first-moment estimate over a finite space, which the preceding published page already develops, and it introduces no rank or independence argument this page reuses.

contents.name: 2.1.1 Fundamental structures (fields, rings)
2.1.2 Polynomials
2.1.3 Linear spaces
2.1.4 Criteria of linear independence
2.2.1 Inequalities for subspaces
2.2.2 Linear maps
2.2.3 Matrices, rank
2.2.4 Systems of linear equations. Affine subspaces
2.2.5 Projective spaces
contents.reason: Projective space over a field is the setting of finite geometry, a subject the library has not reached at this point in the reading order; no bound on this page quantifies over lines or points of a projective space.

contents.name: 2.2.6 Extending the field
contents.reason: Base change along a field extension needs algebraic field extensions, which are not among this page’s declared prerequisites; every theorem here fixes one field in its own statement, which is exactly the discipline the page is trying to enforce.

contents.name: 2.3.1 Inner product spaces (the standard bilinear form over an arbitrary field)
2.3.2 Eventown revisited (the totally isotropic subspace argument)
2.4.1 Notation, terminology (graphs and set systems)
2.4.2 Chromatic number and short cycles
2.4.3 Block designs
contents.reason: Balanced incomplete block designs and their parameter identities are the subject of a planned page of their own, which sits immediately above this one in the reading order and can cite the Fisher bound proved here; defining designs here would put the definition on the wrong side of that citation.

contents.name: 4.1 When all intersections are equal size (the nonuniform Fisher inequality)
4.2 Ramsey theory – a constructive lower bound
contents.reason: The explicit Ramsey graph is built from the modular Frankl–Wilson bound, whose proof needs intersection sizes read modulo a prime and a polynomial space over F_p; that modular machinery is a development of its own and nothing else on this page uses it.

contents.name: 4.3 Restricted intersections (the nonuniform Ray-Chaudhuri–Wilson bound)
4.4 Extremal set theory: the classics (Sperner, Erdős–Ko–Rado, Kruskal–Katona)
contents.reason: These are pure-counting theorems about antichains and intersecting families proved by shifting and by compression, not by rank arguments; Erdős–Ko–Rado and Kruskal–Katona in particular need the shadow apparatus, and putting them here would misfile them under the linear-algebra method they do not use.

contents.name: 7.1 The inclusion matrix; s-independent families
7.2 Extended inclusion matrices. The Nonuniform RW Theorem revisited
contents.reason: The extended inclusion matrix route needs the rank of W_{t,k}(n) over the whole range t <= k <= n-t, whose boundary case k = n-t is the nonsingularity of the disjointness matrix; the known proofs of that go through eigenvalues of the Johnson scheme or Gottlieb’s construction, neither of which is available here. The same bound is obtained on this page by the multilinear polynomial route instead.

contents.name: 7.3 Inclusion matrices of uniform families (the sharp uniform Ray-Chaudhuri–Wilson bound)
contents.reason: The uniform bound binom(n,s) is genuinely stronger than the nonuniform one and is not a corollary of it; its proof needs the higher inclusion matrices of this section together with Gottlieb’s rank theorem, so it is blocked by exactly the rank result declined above.

contents.name: 7.4 Linear dependencies among the rows of inclusion matrices and the Vapnik–Chervonenkis dimension
7.5 Shadows of s-independent families
contents.reason: The shadow bound is a statement about the family of subsets of the members of a family and needs the shadow operator with its Kruskal–Katona-style estimates; no theorem on this page takes a shadow, so the operator would be introduced with no consumer.

sources.title: J. Matoušek, Thirty-three Miniatures: Mathematical and Algorithmic Applications of Linear Algebra (AMS preliminary version)

contents.name: Miniature 1. Fibonacci Numbers, Quickly
contents.reason: This is an algorithmic observation about computing a Fibonacci number by repeated squaring of a matrix; it is about the cost of a computation, and the library records no model of computation in which such a cost can be stated.

contents.name: Miniature 2. Fibonacci Numbers, the Formula
Miniature 3. The Clubs of Oddtown
Miniature 4. Same-Size Intersections (the generalized Fisher inequality)
Miniature 5. Error-Correcting Codes (the Hamming code)
contents.reason: Linear codes need the code, its minimum distance and its parity-check matrix as defined objects, and error correction needs the decoding statement; none of the bounds on this page mentions a code, so the whole apparatus would arrive for one example.

contents.name: Miniature 6. Odd Distances (at most n+2 points in the plane with pairwise odd distances)
contents.reason: The argument attaches a Gram matrix of squared distances and works modulo 2 inside a quadratic form over the rationals; it needs Euclidean distance in the plane and 2-adic valuation of rationals together, and this page carries no metric.

contents.name: Miniature 7. Are These Distances Euclidean? (the Schoenberg criterion)
contents.reason: Realising a distance matrix by points of R^n is a statement about positive semidefinite matrices and their square roots; the semidefinite square root is the missing ingredient and it belongs with the spectral theorem rather than with set-system bounds.

contents.name: Miniature 8. Packing Complete Bipartite Graphs (Graham–Pollak)
Miniature 9. Equiangular Lines (at most binom(d+1,2) of them in R^d)
contents.reason: Equiangular lines are a statement about one-dimensional subspaces of R^d at a fixed angle, and the proof works inside the space of symmetric matrices with the trace form; that is a second inner-product space beyond the coordinate one this page uses, introduced for a single result.

contents.name: Miniature 10. Where is the Triangle? (detecting a triangle by matrix multiplication)
contents.reason: The result is a statement about an algorithm’s running time expressed through fast matrix multiplication; there is no model of computation here in which "faster" is a proposition.

contents.name: Miniature 11. Checking Matrix Multiplication (Freivalds’ algorithm)
contents.reason: A randomised verification procedure whose statement is about the probability that a randomised algorithm errs, which needs a probabilistic model of an algorithm rather than of a finite sample space alone.

contents.name: Miniature 12. Tiling a Rectangle by Squares
contents.reason: The classical proof uses a discontinuous additive function on the reals obtained from a Hamel basis, and the statement is about geometric tilings of a rectangle; both the geometry and the Hamel-basis construction sit outside this page.

contents.name: Miniature 13. Three Petersens Are Not Enough (K_10 is not the union of three Petersen graphs)
contents.reason: The proof computes the spectrum of the Petersen graph and uses eigenvalue interlacing, so it needs the adjacency matrix and the spectral theorem; the planned spectral graph theory page is where the adjacency spectrum is developed and it sits above this one.

contents.name: Miniature 14. Petersen, Hoffman–Singleton, and Maybe 57 (Moore graphs of diameter two)
contents.reason: The classification of Moore graphs rests on integrality of the eigenvalue multiplicities of the adjacency matrix, which is the same spectral apparatus, and its endgame is a divisibility argument about those multiplicities.

contents.name: Miniature 15. Only Two Distances (point sets in R^d realising only two distances)
contents.reason: The bound comes from independence of the polynomials x -> prod (|x-p|^2 - d_i^2) on the point set, so it needs the Euclidean norm on R^d as the argument of the polynomials; the multilinear machinery this page builds lives on the discrete cube instead.

contents.name: Miniature 16. Covering a Cube Minus One Vertex
Miniature 17. Medium-Size Intersection Is Hard To Avoid (the Frankl–Wilson inequality)

contents.name: 2. Lindstrom's Theorem (m >= n+2 subsets of [n] admit disjoint I_1, I_2 with equal unions and equal intersections)
contents.reason: The theorem is a genuine linear-algebra-method result, but its proof runs inside the subspace of R^{2n} cut out by x_j + y_j constant and reads the conclusion off which coordinates are nonzero; it introduces the doubled incidence vector, an object no other bound on this page uses, and the page already carries three independence criteria that it would only illustrate.

contents.name: 3.1 {0,1,*}-Addressing (addressing a graph into the squashed cube)
contents.reason: The addressing problem needs the squashed cube and its distance function as defined objects; the linear-algebra content is the Graham–Pollak bound, which is included, and the addressing formulation is what that bound was originally about rather than a further theorem.

contents.name: 3.2 Reduction to Decompositions (complete bipartite decompositions of a graph)
3.3 Graham–Pollack Theorem
4.1 A Few Problems (the Oddtown and Eventown rules)
4.2 Solutions (the rank and isotropic-subspace arguments)
5. Modular Frankl–Wilson Inequality
contents.reason: The modular bound replaces "intersection size lies in L" by "intersection size lies in L modulo p" and needs polynomials over F_p together with a uniformity hypothesis on the family; the hypotheses look like the integer ones and are not, so importing it without its own development is exactly the confusion the page is trying to avoid.

contents.name: 11.1 Cauchy–Davenport Theorem
11.2 Regular Subgraphs (a graph of large average and bounded maximum degree has a p-regular subgraph)
contents.reason: The proof applies the Nullstellensatz to a polynomial built from the vertex-edge incidence matrix over F_p and needs the incidence matrix of a graph together with degree bookkeeping modulo p; that is a second incidence object beyond the set-family one this page defines.

contents.name: 11.3 Covering Cube by Affine Hyperplanes
11.4 Chevalley–Warning Theorem
contents.reason: Chevalley–Warning counts common zeros of a system over a finite field F_q modulo p, so it needs F_q for a prime power q and the sum of x^k over the field; the library has the prime fields Z/p but not the general finite field at this point in the reading order.

contents.name: 11.5 Sets Meeting Every Affine Hyperplane
contents.reason: The statement quantifies over affine hyperplanes of F_q^n and its proof is a dimension count in a polynomial space over F_q, so it is blocked by the same absence of the general finite field.

sources.title: N. Alon, "Combinatorial Nullstellensatz", Combinatorics, Probability and Computing 8 (1999) 7–29

contents.name: Theorem 1.1 (Combinatorial Nullstellensatz I: membership in the ideal generated by the grid polynomials)
contents.reason: The ideal-membership form asserts f = sum h_i g_i with degree control and a coefficient-subring clause; it needs ideals in a multivariate polynomial ring and a division statement in several variables, and the applications on this page all go through the coefficient form instead.

contents.name: Theorem 1.2 (Combinatorial Nullstellensatz II: the nonvanishing criterion)
Lemma 2.1 (a polynomial with small degree in each variable vanishing on a grid is zero)
Theorem 3.1 (Chevalley–Warning: p divides the number of common zeros)
contents.reason: The statement is over F_q for a prime power q and its proof sums a polynomial over the whole field; the library supplies the prime fields Z/p and not F_q, and stating it only for q = p would misreport the theorem.

contents.name: Theorem 3.2 (Cauchy–Davenport)
Theorem 6.1 (a graph with average degree above 2p-2 and maximum degree at most 2p-1 has a p-regular subgraph)
